Although guidance methods have been developed to mitigate these issues, they are primarily designed for autoregressive models and do not directly apply to in-place editing (Peng et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024b). Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a natural interface for these tasks because they are not restricted to next-token prediction and can generate tokens anywhere on the shared canvas (Austin et al., 2021; Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024a). As illustrated in Figure 1, the missing output regions are initially masked and progressively filled, while demonstrations and surrounding context remain visible. passages.text: Multi-Target Few-Shot Prompting with Diffusion Language Models Anton Xue, Alan Li, and Rahul Saha University of Texas at Austin anton.xue@utexas.edu alan.li@cs.utexas.edu rahul.saha@utexas.edu github.com/AntonXue/fewshot-dlms Abstract Few-shot prompting is useful when instructions and rewards are hard to specify. One such application is editing by example, where a demonstrated formatting change or API migration may need to be applied across multiple sites. However, such edits often depend on both left and right context, making generation with causal autoregressive models awkward. We therefore introduce multi-target few-shot prompting with diffusion language models, where examples guide the infilling of multiple masked regions
passages.label: 相关段落：第 1 页

passages.text: models (Li et al., 2023; O’Brien and Lewis, 2023), while context-aware methods compare predictions under different conditioning contexts to strengthen the influence of supplied evidence or demonstrations (Peng et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024b; Song et al., 2025; Whitammer et al., 2022). In diffusion models, classifier-free guidance adjusts the influence of conditioning information (Ho and Salimans, 2021), while KL-regularized reward tilting (Korbak et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023) and inference-time resampling (Singhal et al., 2025) provide mechanisms for reweighting candidate generations. However, extending likelihood-based comparisons to complete DLM infills requires tractable sequence-level likelihoods under a specified decoding procedure. Diffusion language models. Masked diffusion language models iteratively unmask positions within a shared canvas, supporting flexible generation orders and parallel decoding (Austin et al., 2021; Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024a).
